stem: A company runs dual-stack Amazon EC2 instances in a private subnet of a VPC that has an IPv6 CIDR block. The instances must download updates from servers on the internet that are reachable over IPv6 addresses. The network path must prevent the internet from starting connections to the instances, whatever their security groups allow. The VPC already has an internet gateway for its public subnets. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?
keywords: prevent the internet from starting connections to the instances

options.text: Create an egress-only internet gateway, and add a route for ::/0 with the egress-only internet gateway as its target to the private route table.
options.why: This is the AWS design for a private subnet: [create a route that routes all internet-bound IPv6 traffic from the subnet to an egress-only internet gateway](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-ipv6-add-step2-routes).

options.text: Add a route for ::/0 with the existing internet gateway as its target to the route table of the private subnet of the instances.
options.why: The route makes the subnet public for IPv6, and [IPv6 addresses are globally unique, and therefore public by default](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-eip-ipv6-not-supported), so the internet can start connections.
options.misconception: an IPv6 address in a private subnet is private, like a private IPv4 address

options.text: Create an egress-only internet gateway, and add a route for 0.0.0.0/0 with the egress-only internet gateway as its target to the private route table.
options.why: The gateway is [for use with IPv6 traffic only](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-eigw-ipv6-outbound-only), and the updates go to IPv6 addresses, which a 0.0.0.0/0 route does not match.

options.text: Launch a fleet of proxy instances in a public subnet, and route ::/0 from the private subnet to the proxies, which forward the update requests.
options.why: It can work, but the team runs, patches and scales a proxy fleet, which is far more work than one managed gateway and one route.
options.misconception: outbound-only IPv6 needs a self-managed proxy

explanation: An egress-only internet gateway [allows outbound communication over IPv6 from instances in your VPC to the internet, and prevents the internet from initiating an IPv6 connection with your instances](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-eigw-ipv6-outbound-only). The gateway is a VPC component, so the team runs no servers for it. The route for ::/0 sends every IPv6 destination on the internet to the gateway.
takeaway: Outbound-only IPv6 uses an egress-only internet gateway; outbound-only IPv4 uses a NAT gateway.
twin: If the stem said "servers that are reachable over IPv4 addresses" instead: a NAT gateway, because AWS says [To enable outbound-only internet communication over IPv4, use a NAT gateway instead](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-eigw-ipv6-outbound-only).
say: For outbound-only IPv6 I'd use an egress-only internet gateway with a ::/0 route.

stem: A company runs 400 Amazon EC2 instances in public subnets. Each instance has a public IPv4 address so that it can download small operating system updates from the internet each night. Nothing on the internet starts connections to the instances. A cost review shows a large monthly charge for public IPv4 addresses. The instances must keep downloading the updates. Which solution will meet these requirements in the MOST cost-effective way?
keywords: Nothing on the internet starts connections to the instances
large monthly charge for public IPv4 addresses

options.text: Replace the public IPv4 address of each instance with an Elastic IP address, so that the address stays the same and is not billed while in use.
options.why: An Elastic IP address is a public IPv4 address too, and [AWS charges for all public IPv4 addresses](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-public-ipv4-charge-2024), in use or idle.

options.text: Remove the public IPv4 addresses, and place an internet-facing Application Load Balancer in front of the instances for their update traffic.
options.why: A load balancer serves traffic that comes in; the instances start outbound connections, and without public addresses they have no egress path.
options.misconception: a load balancer gives its targets outbound internet access

options.text: Move the instances to private subnets without public IPv4 addresses, and send their outbound traffic through NAT gateways in public subnets.
options.why: A few NAT gateways replace hundreds of billed addresses, and AWS points to this pattern: [use Elastic Load Balancers and NAT Gateways for ingress and egress traffic](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-public-ipv4-avoid-per-instance-with-elb-nat).

options.text: Move the instances to private subnets with NAT gateways, and convert each public IPv4 address to an Elastic IP address that stays allocated for a rollback.
options.why: The updates still work, but [The price is the same whether the public IPv4 address is in-use](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-public-ipv4-hourly-in-use-or-idle) or idle, so the kept addresses still cost money.
options.misconception: an Elastic IP address that is not attached to an instance is free

explanation: Every public IPv4 address is billed: [You pay an hourly rate for each public IPv4 address used by your AWS account](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-public-ipv4-hourly-in-use-or-idle). The instances start all their connections themselves, so they need egress, not public addresses. AWS points to this design to lower the charge: [use Elastic Load Balancers and NAT Gateways for ingress and egress traffic](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-public-ipv4-avoid-per-instance-with-elb-nat).
takeaway: Instances that start every connection themselves belong in private subnets behind a NAT gateway, without public IPv4 addresses.
twin: If the stem said "users on the internet call a web application on the instances" instead: an internet-facing load balancer in front of private instances, because AWS suggests [use Elastic Load Balancers and NAT Gateways for ingress and egress traffic](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-public-ipv4-avoid-per-instance-with-elb-nat).
say: Every public IPv4 address costs money, so I'd move outbound-only instances behind a NAT gateway.

stem: A company runs Amazon EC2 instances in a private subnet. A previous administrator associated an Elastic IP address with each instance, but the instances still cannot download the updates that they need to patch their operating systems. The route table of the private subnet has the local route and no other routes. The VPC also has an internet gateway and a public subnet whose route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to the internet gateway. Which solution will let the instances download the updates MOST securely?
keywords: Elastic IP address with each instance
has the local route and no other routes

options.text: Add a 0.0.0.0/0 route to the internet gateway in the route table of the private subnet, and keep the Elastic IP addresses on the instances.
options.why: It works, but the subnet becomes public, and the instances can then receive connections from the internet whenever a security group rule allows them.
options.misconception: a security group gives the same protection as a private subnet

options.text: Add an outbound rule that allows HTTPS to 0.0.0.0/0 to the security groups of the instances, and keep the Elastic IP addresses.
options.why: The missing piece is a route: [instances in the private subnet can't communicate with the internet, even if they have public IP addresses](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-public-vs-private-subnet-by-igw-route).

options.text: Create a zonal NAT gateway in the private subnet, add a 0.0.0.0/0 route to it in the private route table, and release the Elastic IP addresses.
options.why: For internet access, [The NAT gateway must be in a public subnet with a route table that routes internet traffic to an internet gateway](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-troubleshoot-route-placement).
options.misconception: a NAT gateway belongs in the subnet of the instances that use it

options.text: Create a NAT gateway in the public subnet, add a 0.0.0.0/0 route to it in the private route table, and release the Elastic IP addresses.
options.why: Outbound access works, and the internet cannot start connections, because [Connections must always be initiated from within the VPC containing the NAT gateway](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-connections-originate-inside-vpc).

explanation: To reach the internet from a private subnet, [create a NAT gateway or launch a NAT instance in a public subnet](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-natgw-route-from-private-subnet) and send 0.0.0.0/0 to it. The Elastic IP addresses have no use there: they [cannot be used on instances in subnets configured to use a NAT gateway or a NAT instance to access the Internet](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-faq-eip-not-behind-nat), so release them.
takeaway: A private subnet reaches the internet through a NAT gateway in a public subnet, not through public IP addresses.
twin: If the stem said "users on the internet must connect to the instances directly" instead: a route to the internet gateway, because [instances in the private subnet can't communicate with the internet, even if they have public IP addresses](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-public-vs-private-subnet-by-igw-route).
say: A public IP isn't enough in a private subnet; I'd add a NAT gateway in a public subnet.
